label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $(W,S)$ be any Coxeter system and let $x<y$ in the Bruhat order. If the Bruhat interval $[x,y]$ is a lattice, then there is a convex polytope $L_{x,y}$ of dimension $\ell(x,y)-1$ whose complete face lattice is isomorphic to $[x,y]$.

title: Theorem

label: conj-TKL is M
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj-TKL is M}
If $[x,y]$ is a lattice Bruhat interval in any Coxeter group, then the coefficients of $P_{x,y}(q)$ form an $M$-sequence.

label: prob:KL-algebra
title: Problem
body_md:
\label{prob:KL-algebra}
For each lattice Bruhat interval $[x,y]$ in a Coxeter group, give a natural construction of a commutative standard graded Artinian algebra $A_{x,y}$ with
\[
 \operatorname{Hilb}(A_{x,y};q)=P_{x,y}(q).
\]
Can such a construction be made compatible with passage to subintervals?
head: environment

label: thm:lattice-characterization
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: lem:rank-2-positivity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rank-2-positivity}
Let $[u,v]=\{u,a,b,v\}$ be a diamond. Then we have a relation 
\[\lambda_{u,b}=\kappa\lambda_{u,a}+\tau\lambda_{a,v},\quad\text{for }\kappa\in\mathbb{R},\ \tau\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}.\]
In particular, for $\varphi\in V_{x,y}$, if $\lambda_{e_1}(\varphi)=\lambda_{e_2}(\varphi)=0$ for two adjacent edges $e_1$ and $e_2$ of this diamond, then $\lambda_e(\varphi)=0$ for every edge $e$ of this diamond.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The coefficients on either saturated chain of the diamond determine the rest. Hence there are scalars $\kappa,\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lambda_{u,b}=\kappa\lambda_{u,a}+\tau\lambda_{a,v}.$

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the positive left coroot labels of $u\lessdot a$, $u\lessdot b$, and $a\lessdot v$, respectively. Evaluating this relation on $\theta_\zeta(w)=-w^{-1}\zeta$ gives $\beta=\kappa\alpha+\tau\gamma$. 

Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are independent, $\tau\neq0$. Choose $\zeta\in\mathfrak h^*$ with $\zeta(\alpha)=0$ and $\zeta(\gamma)=1$. Order positive coroots by $\zeta(\rho)/\eta(\rho)$, breaking ties lexicographically using fixed linear coordinates of $\beta/\eta(\beta)$. This is a reflection order \cite[Section~2.2]{Dyer-Hecke}. The chain $u\lessdot a\lessdot v$ is strictly increasing, so it is lexicographically first \cite[Proposition~4.3]{Dyer-Hecke}. Its first label is $0$, whereas the first label of the other chain is $\zeta(\beta)/\eta(\beta)=\tau/\eta(\beta)$. Therefore $\tau>0$.
head: environment

label: lem:lattice-bruhat-dimension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lattice-bruhat-dimension}
Let $[x,y]$ be a lattice Bruhat interval of rank $n$. Then $\dim V_{x,y}=n$. Moreover, for any maximal chain $x=x_0\lessdot x_1\lessdot\cdots\lessdot x_{n}=y$, the map $\oplus_{i=1}^n\lambda_{x_{i-1},x_{i}}:V_{x,y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^n$ is a linear isomorphism of vector spaces.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: It is clear that this map is linear. By Dyer \cite{Dyer97} and Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-characterization}, $\dim V_{x,y}=-[q^{\ell(x,y)-1}]R_{x,y}(q)=n$. It then suffices to show that this map is injective. Since this chain diamond generates, by Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-2-positivity}, for $\varphi\in V_{x,y}$, if $\lambda_{x_{i-1},x_{i}}(\varphi)=0$ for all $i\in[n]$, then indeed $\lambda_{w,wt}(\varphi)=0$ for all edges $(w,wt)$ of the Bruhat graph.
head: environment

label: def:fc
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:fc}
For each coatom $c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y)$, define $f^c\in V_{x,y}$ such that $\lambda_{x_{i-1},x_i}(f^c)=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,n-1$ and $\lambda_{c,y}(f^c)=1$, where $x=x_0\lessdot x_1\lessdot\cdots\lessdot x_{n-1}=c\lessdot y$ is a maximal chain. This definition does not depend on the choice of maximal chain from $x$ to $c$.
head: environment

title: Example
head: environment

label: lem:positivity-main
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:positivity-main}
Let $[x,y]$ be a lattice Bruhat interval and define $f^c$ for $c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:fc}. For an atom $a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y)$, $\lambda_a(f^c)>0$ if $a\nleq c$ and $\lambda_a(f^c)=0$ if $a\leq c$.
head: environment

label: lem:short-ordinary-sections
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:short-ordinary-sections}
Let $[x,y]$ be a lattice Bruhat interval with $1\leq\ell(x,y)\leq3$. Every $\varphi\in V_{x,y}$ is represented by $w\mapsto-w^{-1}\zeta$ for some $\zeta\in\mathfrak h^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $n=\ell(x,y)$ and choose a maximal chain $x=x_0\lessdot x_1\lessdot\cdots\lessdot x_n=y$, and let $\beta_i$ be the positive left coroot label of $x_{i-1}\lessdot x_i$. We claim that $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n$ are linearly independent. There is nothing to do if $n\leq2$ so assume $n=3$. If $\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3$ are linearly dependent, then their span $V$ has dimension $2$ and their corresponding reflections generate a dihedral subgroup. All the left coroot labels in $[x,y]$ are in the span $V$ since the maximal chains are connected by diamond flips. The whole interval $[x,y]$ must be isomorphic to a subinterval of the Bruhat order of a dihedral group (see for example \cite[Theorem~1.4]{Dyer-Bruhat-graph}), which has to be a $2$-crown since $\ell(x,y)=3$, contradicting $[x,y]$ being a lattice.

Since $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n$ are linearly independent, we can choose $\zeta\in\mathfrak{h}^*$ so that $\zeta(\beta_i)=\lambda_{x_{i-1},x_i}(\varphi)$ for all $i$. Define $\theta_{\zeta}\in V_{x,y}$ by $\theta_{\zeta}(w)=-w^{-1}\zeta$. As in the calculation for $\theta$, we have $\theta_{\zeta}(wt)-\theta_\zeta(w)=\zeta(w\alpha_t^{\vee})\alpha_t$. Therefore, $\theta_{\zeta}$ and $\varphi$ agree on this maximal chain, and thus agree everywhere.
head: environment

label: lem:sublevel-connectivity
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Call $\varphi$ \emph{generic} if $\lambda_e(\varphi)/\lambda_e(\theta)\neq\lambda_{e'}(\varphi)/\lambda_{e'}(\theta)$ whenever $\lambda_e/\lambda_e(\theta)$ and $\lambda_{e'}/\lambda_{e'}(\theta)$ are distinct functionals. Note that when the left coroot labels $\beta_e$ and $\beta_{e'}$ are distinct, then they indeed provide distinct functionals. Such generic sections form a dense open subset of $V_{x,y}$, since only finitely many proper hyperplanes are excluded. We first assume that $\varphi$ is generic, and label each cover edge $e$ by $\lambda_e(\varphi)/\lambda_e(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}$, reading chains from bottom to top. We now show that each subinterval of rank at most $3$ has a unique strictly increasing maximal chain, whose label sequence is lexicographically minimal among all maximal chains in that subinterval.

For a subinterval of rank at most $3$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:short-ordinary-sections}, $\varphi$ is represented by $w\mapsto -w^{-1}\zeta$ for some $\zeta\in\mathfrak{h}^*$ locally. Consequently, the label of an edge $e$ in this subinterval is $\zeta(\beta_e)/\eta(\beta_e)$. Order the positive coroots by these ratios, breaking ties lexicographically using fixed linear coordinates of $\beta/\eta(\beta)$. Since normalization by $\eta$ turns positive linear combinations into convex combinations, this is a reflection order by \cite[Section~2.2]{Dyer-Hecke}. Genericity ensures that its comparisons on distinct coroots occurring in the subinterval agree with the numerical labels. The assertion therefore follows from \cite[Proposition~4.3]{Dyer-Hecke},
using inversion to pass to left labels. 

We then analyze maximal chains in $[x,y]$ with the numerical labels. A \emph{descent flip} replaces a decreasing two-edge segment of a maximal chain by the other side of its diamond. Such a flip strictly decreases the label sequence lexicographically. Since there are finitely many maximal chains, every sequence of descent flips terminates. Successive edges have distinct left coroot labels and hence distinct numerical labels, so a terminal chain is strictly increasing. We claim that the terminal chain is independent of all choices. Suppose two descent flips are available at the same chain. If their two-edge segments do not overlap in an edge, the flips commute. Otherwise, both segments lie in a rank-three subinterval. After either first flip, further descent flips within that subinterval terminate at its unique increasing maximal chain, while leaving the rest unchanged. Thus the two resulting chains have a common descendant. Since descent flips terminate and are locally confluent, Newman's lemma \cite[Theorem~3]{Newman1942} (also called Rome's lemma) implies that every maximal chain has a unique terminal chain. Finally, maximal chains are connected by diamond flips, and each diamond flip is a descent flip in one direction. Therefore all maximal chains have the same terminal chain.

We can now prove the connectivity in the original lemma statement. Let $a_0$ be the first atom of the common terminal chain that is strictly increasing. Starting from a maximal chain through any atom $a$, perform descent flips and record the atoms inside. Each flip either leaves the atom unchanged or replaces it by an adjacent atom with strictly smaller height. This gives a path from $a$ to $a_0$ in the atom graph $A(x,y)$ along which $\lambda_a(\varphi)/\lambda_a(\theta)$ strictly decreases. Thus, each of the nonempty sets in the lemma statement contains $a_0$, and each of its vertices is connected to $a_0$ within the set.

Finally, let $\varphi$ be arbitrary and consider either selected set of atoms. The empty and full sets cause no difficulty. Otherwise, every selected height is strictly smaller than every unselected height. Choose a threshold strictly between these two finite sets of heights, and perturb $\varphi$ to a sufficiently close generic section.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By construction, $\lambda_{w,wt}(f^c)=0$ if $w<wt\leq c$. In particular, $\lambda_a(f^c)=0$ for $a\leq c$. The interesting part is showing $\lambda_a(f^c)>0$ for $a\nleq c$.

We induct on $n=\ell(x,y)$. The base case $n=2$ follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-2-positivity}. 

Consider an edge $a\sim b$ of $A(x,y)$ with $a\nleq c$ and $b\leq c$, and put $z=a\vee b$. Then $[x,z]=\{x,a,b,z\}$ is a diamond.  Since $z\in\operatorname{At}(b,y)$ and $z\nleq c$, the induction hypothesis applied to the restriction of $f^c$ to $[b,y]$ gives $\lambda_{b,z}(f^c)>0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:rank-2-positivity} therefore implies
\[
\lambda_a(f^c)=\kappa\lambda_b(f^c)+\tau\lambda_{b,z}(f^c)=\tau\lambda_{b,z}(f^c)>0,\qquad \text{for }\tau>0.
\]
Thus every edge leaving the atoms below $c$ has a strictly positive outside endpoint.

Now consider the set
\[
S_c=\{a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y):\lambda_a(f^c)\leq0\}.
\]
Since normalizing by $\lambda_a(\theta)>0$ does not change the sign, Lemma~\ref{lem:sublevel-connectivity} says that its induced subgraph is connected. It contains the nonempty set of atoms below $c$. If it also contained an atom outside $c$, a path within $S_c$ starting below $c$ would have a first edge leaving $c$. Its outside endpoint has strictly positive evaluation by the preceding paragraph, a contradiction. Hence $S_c=\{b\in\operatorname{At}(x,y):b\leq c\}$, proving the desired strict positivity.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a lattice Bruhat interval $[x,y]$, we show that the complete face lattice of $C_{x,y}$, which is also the complete face lattice of $L_{x,y}$, is isomorphic to $[x,y]$.

Note that $[x,y]$ is atomic, i.e. every element is the join of atoms below it. This is because every $z\in[x,y]$ with $\ell(x,z)\geq2$ has at least two elements $z_1$ and $z_2$ covered by $z$ so that $z=z_1\vee z_2$ and then we can apply induction to $z_1$ and $z_2$. Similarly, $[x,y]$ is coatomic, meaning that every element is the meet of coatoms above it.

For $z\in[x,y]$, put $K_z:=\mathrm{cone}\{\lambda_a:a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y),a\leq z\}$, so that $K_y=C_{x,y}$. We show 
\[K_z=C_{x,y}\cap\bigcap_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),c\geq z}\ker(f^c).\]
The $\subseteq$ direction follows from $\lambda_a\in\ker(f^c)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:positivity-main}) for $a\le z\leq c$ where $a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y)$ and $c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y)$. For the $\supseteq$ direction, take an element $\sum_{a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y)}c_a\lambda_a$, $c_a\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$ on the right hand side. In order for it to be in $\ker(f^c)$ for a fixed coatom $c\geq z$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:positivity-main}, we must have that $c_b=0$ if $b\nleq c$. Any atom $a$ with $c_a>0$ must lie below every coatom $c\geq z$, and hence below $z=\bigwedge_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),c\geq z}c$ by coatomicity. 

Thus the $K_z$'s are faces of $C_{x,y}$. Clearly for $z\leq z'$, $K_z\subseteq K_{z'}$. Also, if $z\lessdot z'$, atomicity implies that $z'=z\vee a$ for some atom $a\nleq z$. Coatomicity says that there exists some coatom $c\ngeq z'$ such that $z=z'\wedge c$. Then $a\nleq c$ and $\lambda_a\notin\ker(f^c)$ which means that $\lambda_a\in K_{z'}\setminus K_z$, $K_z\subsetneq K_{z'}$. At the same time, $K_{z}=K_{z'}\cap\ker(f^c)$ so $\dim(K_{z'})-\dim(K_z)\geq1$. Together with $V_{x,y}^*$ having dimension $\ell(x,y)$, we deduce that $\dim(K_z)=\ell(x,z)$ for all $z\in[x,y]$. We calculate that 
\[K_{z_1}\cap K_{z_2}=C_{x,y}\cap\bigcap_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),\ c\geq z_1\text{ or }c\geq z_2}\ker(f^c)=K_{z}\]
where $z=\bigwedge_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),\ c\geq z_1\text{ or }c\geq z_2}c=\left(\bigwedge_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),c\geq z_1}c\right)\wedge\left(\bigwedge_{c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y),c\geq z_2}c\right)=z_1\wedge z_2$. In particular, the equation $K_{z_1}\cap K_{z_2}=K_{z_1\wedge z_2}$ implies that all the $K_z$'s are distinct faces, by dimensional considerations. Then if $K_{z}\subseteq K_{z'}$, $K_z=K_z\cap K_{z'}=K_{z\wedge z'}$, $z=z\wedge z'$ so $z\leq z'$. Thus, $z\mapsto K_z$ is an order embedding from $[x,y]$ to $\mathcal{F}(C_{x,y})$.

Finally, there are no additional faces. It is a well-known fact that all maximal chains in the complete face lattice of a polytope are connected by diamond flips. See for example \cite{Bayer-Barycentric}, or use Balinski's theorem \cite[Theorem~3.14]{Ziegler} to establish that the facet-adjacency graph is connected and apply induction. Starting from any maximal chain $K_{z_0}\subsetneq K_{z_1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq K_{z_n}$, all possible diamond flips can involve only some other known face $K_{z'}$, as all rank $2$ Bruhat intervals are diamonds. Therefore, all faces of $C_{x,y}$ are known.
head: environment

label: prop:toric-Richardson
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: cor:geometric-realization
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:geometric-realization}
The complete face lattice of the rational $(n-1)$-polytope $\Pi_{x,y}$ is $[x,y]$. Furthermore, there is a projective toric $(n-1)$-fold $X_{x,y}$ with moment polytope $\Pi_{x,y}$ and
\[
X_{x,y}=\bigsqcup_{x<w\leq y}O_w,\qquad O_w\subseteq\overline{O_z}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ w\leq z, \qquad \dim O_w=\ell(x,w)-1.
\]
Thus $[x,y]$ is the poset of torus-orbit closures in $X_{x,y}$, with the empty set adjoined. For $n\geq2$, $X_{x,y}$ is the new invariant divisor in a projective toric modification of $\overline{R}_{x,y}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A face $[a,b]$ of $Q_{x,y}$ satisfies $x\le a\le b\le y$. It contains $q_x=[x, x]$ precisely when $a\leq x\leq b$, hence precisely when $a=x$. The interval of faces containing $q_x$ is therefore
\[
 \{[x,w]:x\leq w\leq y\}\cong[x,y].
\]
Taking the vertex figure identifies $q_x$ with the empty face of $\Pi_{x,y}$, and the face $[x,w]$ of $Q_{x,y}$, for $w>x$, with a face of $\Pi_{x,y}$ of dimension $\ell(x,w)-1$. This proves the first assertion; compare \cite[Corollary~6.8]{BossingerGorskySimental2026}.

Choose a positive integral dilation making $\Pi_{x,y}$ a lattice polytope. Its normal fan defines a projective toric variety, and the assertions about its orbits follow from the orbit-cone correspondence \cite[Theorem 3.2.6]{CLS2011}. For $n\geq2$, truncate $Q_{x,y}$ at $q_x$ by setting
\[
 Q'_{x,y}=Q_{x,y}\cap \{\lambda\leq\lambda(q_x)-\varepsilon\}.
\]
The normal fan of $Q'_{x,y}$ refines the normal fan of $Q_{x,y}$. The resulting projective equivariant toric modification 
$$X_{Q'_{x,y}}\longrightarrow X_{Q_{x,y}}=\overline{R}_{x,y}$$
creates a new torus-invariant divisor $X_{x,y}$ whose moment polytope is exactly $\Pi_{x,y}$ (see the constructions of projective toric varieties and fan refinements in \cite{CLS2011}). For $n=1$, the variety $X_{x,y}$ is a point; no exceptional divisor construction is needed.
head: environment

label: thm:Richardson-IH
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The local intersection cohomology of a toric orbit closure in a projective toric variety is computed by the right KLS polynomial of its orbit-closure interval \cite{DenefLoeser1991,Fieseler1991} (see also \cite[Corollary~4.20]{Proudfoot2018}). Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:toric-Richardson} gives the vanishing in odd degrees and the first equality in the local formula. The local product theorem for Richardson varieties \cite[Section~3.1, p.~397]{KnutsonWooYong2013} gives the second equality.

For a projective toric variety with moment polytope $Q$, Stanley's toric $h$-polynomial $h(Q^*,q)$ computes the Poincar\'e polynomial of its global intersection cohomology, in our convention (see \cite{DenefLoeser1991,Fieseler1991}). Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:toric-Richardson} gives the vanishing in odd degrees and the second equality in the global situation. The Poincar\'e polynomial of the global intersection cohomology of any closed Richardson variety $\overline{R}_{x, y}$ (not necessarily toric) can be computed using the classical KL polynomials (see the Richardson $Z$-polynomial formula of \cite[Theorem~4.3 and Remark~4.4]{Proudfoot2018}). This gives the last equality in the global formula.
head: environment

label: thm:rational-smoothness
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A toric variety is rationally smooth precisely when its fan is simplicial \cite[Theorem~11.4.8]{CLS2011}. Since the fan of $\overline{R}_{x,y}$ is the normal fan of $Q_{x,y}$, (1) and (2) are equivalent. In particular, (1), equivalently, (2), implies (3) and (4).

The local intersection cohomology polynomial at a toric fixed point is the toric $g$-polynomial of a section of the corresponding full-dimensional cone. For a $d$-polytope $P$, the linear coefficient of the toric $g$-polynomial is $f_0(P)-(d+1)$ (see, for example, \cite[(5), p.~1153]{Braden2006}). Since a toric $g$-polynomials cannot have internal zeros, it follows that this local polynomial is $1$ if and only if the cone is simplicial. Hence (3) says that $q_x$ is a simple vertex. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
Its vertex figure $\Pi_{x,y}$ is then a simplex, so (3) implies (8). The same argument at $q_y$, 
                                                                                                                                                                                               
whose vertex figure has complete face lattice anti-isomorphic to $[x,y]$, shows that (4) implies (9).

                                                                                                                                                   
By Corollary~\ref{cor:geometric-realization}, (8) and (9) are equivalent. 

If $[x,y]\cong B_n$, then its interval poset is the face lattice of the $n$-cube: a pair of subsets $A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]$ specifies the cube face whose coordinates in $A$ are $1$, those outside $B$ are $0$, and those in $B\setminus A$ are free. This combined with Proposition~\ref{prop:toric-Richardson} proves (9) implies (6), which implies (2). Conversely, a vertex figure of a cube is a simplex, so (6) implies (8).

By Theorem~\ref{thm:Richardson-IH}, $f_{[x,x],[x,y]}(q)=P_{x,y}(q)$. Thus (3) and (5) are equivalent. This establishes all the equivalences except (7).

Note that Stanley's toric $h$-polynomial $h(P,q)$ depends only on the face lattice and by the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Richardson-IH}, we have $H_{x,y}(q)=h(Q_{x,y}^*,q)$ in our convention, where $Q_{x,y}^*$ is the polar dual of $Q_{x,y}$. Hence $h(C_n^*,q)=(1+q)^n$ for an $n$-cube shows that (6) implies (7). 

Conversely, suppose (7) holds and $n\geq2$. For a projective toric $n$-fold with moment polytope $Q$, the coefficient of $q$ in its intersection cohomology Poincar\'e polynomial is $f_{n-1}(Q)-n$, where $f_{n-1}(Q)$ is the number of facets of $Q$. Equivalently, this is the linear coefficient of the toric $h$-polynomial  of the polar polytope (see \cite{Stanley1987}). 
                                                                                                                                 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:toric-Richardson}, the facets in $\operatorname{Int}([x,y])$ are $[x,c]$ and $[a,y]$, with $c\in\operatorname{Co}(x,y)$ and $a\in\operatorname{At}(x,y)$. Thus
\[
 \#\operatorname{At}(x,y)+\#\operatorname{Co}(x,y)=2n.
\]
                                                                                                                                                                                                     
These are the numbers of vertices and facets, respectively, of the $(n-1)$-polytope $\Pi_{x,y}$. 
                                                                            
Each is at least $n$. Consequently $\Pi_{x,y}$ has exactly $n$ vertices, so it is a simplex. The case $n=1$ is immediate. 

Finally, rational smoothness identifies ordinary and intersection cohomology, which proves the last assertion.
head: environment

label: rmk:convention
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:convention}
One needs to distinguish the normal-fan convention for a moment polytope from the face-fan convention (see also \cite[Remark 4.21]{Proudfoot2018}). Our convention is that the toric $g$-vector and the toric $h$-vector extend the simplicial $g$-vector and the simplicial $h$-vector. For example, if $C_n$ is an $n$-cube, then $h(C_n^*,q)=(1+q)^n$, which computes the intersection cohomology Poincar\'e polynomial of the toric variety associated with the normal fan of $C_n$.
head: environment

label: cor:local-toric-KL
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:local-toric-KL}
Let $[x,y]$ be a lattice Bruhat interval in a finite Weyl group. For the projective toric variety $X_{x,y}$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:geometric-realization}, one has
\[
 P_{w,y}(q)=\sum_{i\geq0}\dim\mathrm{IH}^{2i}_p(X_{x,y})q^i \qquad(x<w\leq y,\ p\in O_w).
\]
In particular, all odd local intersection cohomology groups of $X_{x,y}$ vanish.

label: prop:kernel-coincidence
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Every subinterval of a lattice is a lattice. By Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-characterization}, its $R$-polynomial is $(q-1)^{\ell(a,b)}$. The two kernels therefore agree on all comparable pairs in $L$. Uniqueness of the right KLS function gives $f_{a,b}(q)=P_{a,b}(q)$. If $a<b$ and $D_{a,b}$ is any polytope with complete face lattice $[a,b]$, then we have $f_{a,b}(q)=g(D_{a,b}^*;q)$ as discussed above. This proves the remaining assertions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $P=L_{x,y}^{*}$, so that $\dim P=n-1$ and
\[
 P_{x,y}(q)=g(P;q).
\]
Then Kalai’s vanishing theorem proves (1).

For $x<z<y$, the face of $P$ corresponding to $z$ has complete face lattice anti-isomorphic to $[z,y]$, while its face figure in $P$ has complete face lattice anti-isomorphic to $[x,z]$. Their toric $g$-polynomials are $P_{z,y}$ and $P_{x,z}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:kernel-coincidence}. Thus Kalai's monotonicity gives (2).

Note that the vertices of $P$ correspond to the coatoms of $[x,y]$. Substitution of $f_0(P)=m$ and $d=n-1$ into the generalized upper bound theorem proves (3).

Note that by Proposition~\ref{prop:kernel-coincidence}, the linear coefficient of the toric $g$-polynomial (see \cite[(5), p.~1153]{Braden2006}) gives the linear coefficient
\begin{equation*}
 [q]P_{x,y}(q)=f_0(P)-n=m-n.
\end{equation*}
Consequently $P_{x,y}(q)=1$ forces $P$ to have exactly $n$ vertices, and hence to be a simplex. Its face lattice, and therefore $[x,y]$, is Boolean. The converse follows from the fact that the toric $g$-polynomial of a simplex is $1$ (see \cite[p.~1153]{Braden2006}). This proves (4).
